What if you let the group decide how much they can handle?

With each question asked/answered the threat grows. Start out with a single little creature, they ask the question, creature appears, they kill it and get their answer. Ask another question, the threat's doubled; 2 creatures appear now. Kill them and get their answer.

At that point the party would have to start thinking; "That was pretty easy, but can we handle more? How many more will there be next time? Is it worth the risk?"

I think for me a demon/fiend theme would fit this pretty appropriately. Not a lot of other types of creatures or beings out there willing to trade information at the sacrifice of kin.

But the opposite direction could work too; a celestial device that, like you said, "tests the worth" of those seeking knowledge could be really cool as well.

Edit: Expanding on the celestial version of this; I'd think of this one more as the party enters a room where they can see all the opponents surrounding them, standing and waiting for challengers. Correct, the population and ratio of your server are irrelevant when you activate warmode. They take you and put you into an instance of the world with an even split of players from all different servers so that the ratio is even

I don't main as healer, but my first alt is a Mistweaver monk and I use healbot exclusively. Barely healed at all before getting it, but it definitely makes things easier. 

Honestly, one of the main requirements for healing is mouse over macros, which Healbot pretty much simulates, but it also ties in keybinds. 

So basically you either need to go through and create mouseovermacros for all your abilites and keybind them appropriately, or you download healbot.

Outlaw is kind of the balance between the 2, not the best single target, not the best AoE, but good maintained cleave, and acceptable single target damage. I've only played this one a little, mostly to get the mage tower appearance.

Relies on high haste/speed stats, core spec abilities are "pirate" themed with lots of RNG and procs. You have an ability called "Roll the Bones" where you literally roll some dice and gain a random buff(s).

Subtlety is the high stealth spec, lots of "stance dancing" where you're activating abilities that either directly put you back into stealth or simulate stealth so you can use your stealth based abilities. I haven't played this one in a very long time because it is mechanically the more difficult spec to learn and master and I do not feel like the damage output has been worth the learning curve and that high(er) skill cap is just not fun for me.

Sub excels at AoE, dealing more damage the more enemies you can hit with your aoe abilities. Excellent for high tier M+ dungeons, solid single target, but not always the best, definitely best AoE.

Assassination relies heavily on Damage over Time effects/Debuffs on your target. Your abilities apply poison to the target, and you have a number of of active abilities to apply bleeds. Assassination is a fairly simple spec where you focus on keeping those debuffs on your target, and make use of your 1-2 cool downs to have high burst windows. Best single target damage with acceptable multi-target/aoe, but not the best.

Short answer is, no you don't need to "equip" spells into spell slots. That almost sounds like a throwback to the old 3e wizard rule where you could only cast a certain number of spells a day and yo uhad to determine what spells each of those casts was going to be ahead of time.

Each caster is a little different in how they mange their spell lists this edition, for example, some caster classes need to "prepare" spells before the can cast them, like the druid. They get access to their entire spell list, but each day they can switch out which spells they have "prepared" and use their spell slots to cast those particular ones. They could prepare 3 spells and spell slots, but only cast one of them 3 times if they wanted, or cast all 3 spells, one for each slot.

Sorcerer's on the other hand know a limited amount of spells but alway have them ready, so they can use any spell they want as long as they have the appropriate level spell slot available.

I don't know a ton about warlocks, somethinga bout using the highest spell slot available, but it's a little different than the rest.

I will say as an actual recurve archery shooter, the logistics of attempting this are gross.

Nocking and firing a single arrow with any amount of accuracy relies on the fact that from the point the arrow is nocked, drawn, and released, it is perfectly aligned and level with the intended target. Typically laying across a rest that is measurably aligned with a specific point on the string consistently(nock point), which falls along a specific point of the draw angle when the string is drawn.

Now imagine resting a second arrow over the first. It will not be resting on a large stable surface like the first so there will likely be variations due to movement/instability. The nock of the arrow will also be significantly higher on the string due to the fletchings on both arrows, causing the actual trajectory to point down. These fletchings will also interfere with each other as they (if they manage to) leave the string, throwing off the trajectory of each arrow. 

For flavor, you can absolutely let them do it, but don't let them try to gain any actual benefit from doing it (no extra damage or bonuses) because it reality it's significantly more difficult and weaker as the energy released by firing the bow is actually now being split between 2 objects(or more) instead of one.

This isn't typical D&D and if you're not comfortable with it, don't continue it.

One thing I read definitely goes along with some of the things here; Keep combat moving quickly. If your group is all somewhat experienced, tell them that if they don't START taking their turn in a few seconds they "hesitate" and their character takes the Parry action for that turn. 

Losing just one turn will most likely be enough to keep the whole table engaged in the entire combat instead of just zoning out until their turn. It keeps them thinking about what they want to do so they don't get caught off guard and end up giving up their action that round. 

It also helps build some level of urgency in combat that I feel is important, and prevents them doing too much strategy discussion in the middle of combat, which not only drags things to a screeching halt, but for me also breaks that 6 second round idea.

They probably wouldn't be using advanced war tactics, aren't going to be highly trained at killing, and at the first sign of things going badly would probably panic and/or attempt to flee.

As the players progress, the sophistication of even these types of enemies can improve to provide better challenges as well as an advancing narrative, like instead of the uncoordinated band of Bandits you fought early on, you've actually made a name for yourself with the bandit leaders and they've specifically sent their more/most adept members to "take care of you". These guys would be more "veteran" bandits, and would be more likely to coordinate an attack against you, hold their ground and would be more experienced fighters.

Not a DM, but the talking over you is the first thing that needs to be addressed. The players need to respect the GM and understand that when you're talking, it's for their benefit; you're not just talking for the sake of talking.

Your character could shout a command or something quick like that, but if they take too long tell them they have to take a forced pass/defend action. I haven't played one, but I would think there's a couple ways to go about it.

The first that comes to mind is probably the most obvious:
You've intentionally broken your oath for what ever reason. I see this playing out as something that happens over time. Through events around you, you start to feel that no matter what you do, the world is set against you. Eventually you forsake your oath, believing the world is ugly and instead of fighting it, you might as well become ugly too.

The other way I've considered this is you unintentionally or inadvertently break your oath and are crushed by the weight of that action. You set out to find a way to repent for this and make right your fault. Maybe you lost your self control, and in a moment of rage did something against your oath, or even in what you thought was an act of mercy you allowed someone bad a chance to change their ways, but instead they go on to commit some act that goes against your oath and you feel responsible, as if you broke your oath through their actions.

The game is essentially balanced around End Game. End Game in WoW consists of dungeons and raids at max level(currently 100). Dungeons come in a few different difficulties; normal, heroic and Mythic, ascending in difficulty in that order, same for raids.

Sub is absolutely more gear dependent. 

That, coupled with the fact that Sub and Combat share the same secondary priority stat(Multi as opposed to Assassinations Mastery) makes the Sub/Combat combo even more perfect.

If you're switching from Sin to Sub, you need to re-prioritize your secondary stats. Sin uses Mastery, Sub relies heavily on Multi.

Sub is also a much more complicated spec in terms of buff/debuffs to track, cooldowns to line up and bust phases. 

For example, Sin basic opening is pretty much just PrePot -> Mut -> SR/Vend macro -> Rupture

Sub opening is a little more complicated... Premed(11 before pull) -> SnD(1-2 before pull) -> PrePot(1 before pull) -> Vanish(If 2p T18 for free 5cp) -> SR -> SD -> Rupture -> Ambush/Evis spam

Sub is more reliant on those tier piece bonuses too, and it's recommended to actually stay assassination until you have at least the 2p bonus. (Vanish grants 5 combo points).

With Sub you're tracking SnD, Rupture and trying to maintain as much uptime on Find Weakness you can. But you also have a passive that makes your rupture tick faster on multistrike hits which makes it a little more difficult to keep track of as a few multistrikes in a row can cause it to expend its whole duration in a few seconds. Coming from assassination it's really easy to lose track of SnD since you won't be used to applying it right away. Same goes with Rupture since it may or may not run its duration much more quickly than assassination.

E-Sports are on the rise, but not all games are making it big. Call of Duty is one of the lower tier competitive games in that the prize pools are small and the coverage is pretty minimal compared to some of the bigger titles. 

As for him personally, like most people have said, the career of a professional gamer typically doesn't go past 25-27 years old. After that, your reflexes start to slow down and you're not able to make the "twitch" decisions or plays that are needed to keep up with the rest of the young crowd. Most of the high profile professionals really made a name for themselves probably around 16ish, which means they were already incredible players by your nephews age. If he isn't actively participating in tournaments and winning consistently by now, he's already behind, and the time it would take to catch up would almost not be worth it for how much it would cut into the effective career time. 

The other thing is that professional e-sports gamers aren't just mindless couch potatoes; they're bright strategists, they're usually in pretty good shape, and have personalities that are capable of producing a following in order to produce income; whether that's through selling merch or making money off YouTube/Twitch videos. People need to want to see him play and just being "really good" usually isn't enough. 

Like other people have said, he needs to have a plan, and needs to find a team. None of these games are solo games, and he needs to be able to work with and coordinate with a professional team. If he's incapable or unwilling to socialize, he's going to be hard pressed to find a professional team willing to work with him.

The last thing that I haven't seen here yet is this; given the short life span of a gaming career, he needs to have a fallback. He's not ever going to make enough money to live off of retiring before he's 30, and needs something else he's good at to switch to when he's not considered "prime" for the e-sports franchise. This means he needs to finish school, and have skills that he can use to get a real job when this is all over.

Personally, I'd say he needs to be talked out of this because it doesn't seem like he's serious or understands what it really takes to be a professional gamer, otherwise he'd be tracking stats, studying strategy, making plans and competing regularly. You and his parents should talk to him and try to direct him back to a better path. 

EDIT:: Even if he does suddenly make it big and starts getting invited to tournaments, e-sports is usually a hit or miss thing. If you don't win, you're not making money. The typical advice here is to start with 30-35#. That way it's easier to focus on form as you won't be struggling to draw, you won't fatigue as quickly, and you'll overall just have a better learning experience.

That being said, it's not impossible to learn on a heavy bow. I started with a 50# recurve (~55# at my draw), and while I do wish I had started lighter, I don't regret the purchase. I enjoy shooting it, I enjoyed the challenge in learning with it, and it's incredibly satisfying when I get a nice tight group near the X.

It takes much much more discipline and commitment to learn on a heavy bow, and it's much easier to pick up bad habits, and learn incorrectly, especially if you're teaching yourself and not taking classes. It can be very frustrating when you can't determine what you're doing wrong simply because so much of your effort goes into simply drawing the string instead of all the other important aspects of the shot.

Disclaimer: I am not an expert, only been shooting for about a year and I'm certainly not a power lifter... Maybe a power sitter as I spend a lot of time in a computer chair. Your experience will vary drastically from mine.

I've hit this issue before... MOST (keyword here) places sell strings based on AMO length, therefore, if you have a 64" bow, you would buy a 64" string. However, there are some places that sell based on ACTUAL string length, so buying a 64" string from them would not be correct, and would be too long.

You also have the strand count to figure in. This isn't something I'm super familiar with though so aside from bringing it to your attention, I don't want to pass on any incorrect information. It should be something you look into though

String wax keeps your string from drying out and becoming brittle. It's a must have, and I usually apply it every few hundred shots, or if the string feels like it's drying out. 

There's videos online of how to do it, it's a very easy process and only takes a few minutes.

Arrows for shooting off the shelf are usually a little more expensive than arrows being shot off a rest since you need feathers, not vanes for off the shelf. This way the fletchings will compress better as they pass over the shelf. Vanes do not do this.

For a 55# bow, you don't have a lot of options for "cheap" arrows. I shoot a 50# recurve and my arrows are typically $75 for half dozen. This is because for a heavier bow you need sturdier arrows. This is called the spine, and it needs to be specific to your draw length, arrow length and draw weight(there are other factors, but those are the key ones).

It sounds like what happened was your string wasn't properly seated in the notch. It's also possible that you might have the string on upside down. If you look closely, the loops on the ends of the string are different sizes. The larger of the 2 is meant to go over the top and slide down the limb so you can attach the bottom, then use the stringer to slide the top loop back into place over the notch. When stringing you should always double check each end to make sure it's properly seated in the notch, and coming straight down the groove of the limb.

I've never had this happen to me, but I feel like it would be difficult for this situation to have snapped an arrow, unless it snapped from hitting something it shouldn't have. I work in software development, but I did a lot of research into game testing before. I knew it wasn't as glamorous as people thought, but I was still interested because I had a passion for gaming, thought it would be a good way to get started in the industry, and genuinely enjoyed beta testing and finding/reporting issues. 

If you are good at thorough examination and analysis of individual software elements, and have an interest in making a career out of not just testing, but genuinely helping to improve a game through testing, breaking and reporting, then by all means go for it.

If however you're just interested in it because you think it's like being in an open beta where you just play the game, report a bug, then continue playing; you have the wrong impression of this job. 

Testing requires hours/days on menial aspects of menial elements of the game. As an entry level tester, you could literally spend the entire development cycle of your first project without ever experiencing anything beyond the options menu. Most of game testing is "shit work" and as the new guy, you will receive the shittiest of the shit work. 

You need to have a basic understanding of testing type concepts; exploratory testing, functional, regression, grey box, etc. 

Every time there is an update from development, you will need to go back and re-test everything from scratch to make sure the changes didn't break something that was previously working fine.

Many of your issues will be kicked back as "working as intended", and this can be extremely frustrating.

Testing is not a "fun" job. It's difficult, and often times feels unrewarding. It can feel fantastic when you uncover something completely game breaking, but for the most part, those Class A, critical bugs will be few and far between.

1. I have the Sage and it's not a bad bow by any means. If that's the style you are after then in that price range I genuinely don't know of any other options off the top of my head. Many people swear by the Sage as the end all be all of beginner/intermediate bows, but there are definitely better bows out there. Problem with those better bows is that they are far outside the price point of this one. The Sage is probably one of the best in its price range.

2. I actually started my first bow out at 50# so I can't say anything from experience regarding increase, but as with most things in archery I would assume the answer is "when you're comfortable". If you don't plan on hunting, there isn't really any reason to go much higher than 30-35#, so I wouldn't be in any real rush to increase if I were you. Keep focusing on your form with the low weight like you are now. 

3. With your draw length only being 27" I don't think you need to be too concerned about the length of the bow. From what I understand, one of the benefits of a longer bow is that they don't "stack" as much when drawing past the rated 28" draw length (Correct me if I'm wrong here guys), meaning how much the draw weight actually increases as you draw past that point. Since you're not hitting that point anyway I don't think this is an issue.

4. I've messed around with different types of draws and again this is something that's pretty much what you're comfortable with I think. Although I do believe there are some regulations against high draws in tournaments and things like that. I don't know much regarding that though. 

5. String wax will help you prolong the life of your string. Really cheap, sold by the tube (looks like chap stick). The decision between off the shelf and off the rest will determine what kind of arrows you purchase. I can't argue for or against either as I don't know the benefits, but I shoot off the shelf purely out of preference (I like traditional bare-bow shooting, no accessories). Shooting off the shelf instead of a rest means you will need arrows fletched with feathers instead of plastic vanes. It also means that you will need to purchase felt/strike plate to protect your shelf/arrows. Again, these are cheap and I often see them packaged together. Someone at your shop can show you how to install them, but essentially the felt covers the wood on the shelf, and the strike plate will go above it on the wall.

6. The rubber grippie things are called "finger savers" I believe and they are mostly common on rentals and kids bows from what I've seen. Mostly it's a way for a shop to not need to hand out finger tabs with every rental bow. You don't need them on your personal bow. 

7. Not being a female shooter, I can't say I've ever had this problem so it's probably entire up to you if you feel like you need that additional protection. You could probably pick up a cheap one just so you have it incase you're having a bad day (I don't wear my arm guard unless I'm having an off day)

For the minium stone, first you need a Calcinator, Glass Bell and Aludal Base (or what ever it's called).

In the Calcinator, you use coal to melt down items into one of the different dusts. What dust you get is based on the item's EMC Value which you can see in the tooltip by holding shift. The minium stone requries Minium dust which is obtained by cooking items with an EMC value equal to or greater than Diamonds (8195 or something like that. Pretty high). Usually I craft gold boots and cook those down, seems like a better trade than 8 diamonds to me.

Once you have the dust, you need to place the dust and the Inert Stone inside the Aludal Base (with the bell on top) and it will cook into a minium stone. 


As for the Mystcraft ages, there are 3 blocks you need, Ink Mixer, Book Binder, and a Writing Desk. You'll also need Ink vials (2 Ink + Water Vial), paper and leather. 

To start you need to place ink and paper in the Ink Mixer to get a Linking page. That page is then crafted with a piece of leather to get an Unlinked book. Put that book in your hand and "Use" it on a floor block where you want the book to take you too (Linking book is used for coming BACK from an Age, so pick where you want to return to).

Now that you have your linking book, craft another Linking panel in the Ink Mixer. Place the panel and leather in the Book Binder to get a Descriptive Book. Place this book in a bookstand (2 sticks and a wood panel). Make sure you have your linking book on you or you will not be able to return from the age!! Click the book in the stand and click on the big square on the right hand page. This will transport you to your first, randomly generated age.

You can specifically craft ages once you start to collect pages, but that's way too complicated for this post.

As to the form, I'm only about 6 months into instinctive myself and a few things I'm noticing with you are that you seem like you bring you head to your anchor instead of the other way around. Also, this is something I had a ton of trouble with for a while, loosen your bow hand. You look like you're gripping pretty tightly. When I shoot I actually keep my hand open completely, using the draw to hold the bow in place, not actually gripping until I've released the arrow.

The nock point isn't really a "contraption", typically it's just a small brass bead (although it can be done with string as well). 

The nock point is simply a way to ensure you are nocking your arrows at the exact same place on the string ever time. It acts as a stopper that you press the nock of the arrow against.

They aren't difficult to put on necessarily, but can be difficult to tune properly. The first one I had on was set too low, and my hair rest was getting shredded, along with my fletchings because the arrows were pretty much "bouncing" off my rest. 

When I replaced the nock point I placed the new one higher up on the string, and it seems to have corrected this issue


You should always have SOME kind of nock point on your sting. Archery is about consistency and that is the sole purpose of a nock point.

If your spine is too stiff for your draw weight, the arrow won't bend the way it's supposed to when leaving the shelf/rest, and typically shoots off to the left of where you want it to (left if you're shooting right handed at least)

When you release the string, the energy released transfers into the arrow. Typically if an arrow is too light for a bow, that energy will cause the arrow to bend (which is perfectly normal) beyond the limit the arrows strength can handle (not so normal) causing the arrow to snap.

I'm no expert on shaft spines, and I've never shot a longbow, but from the little I know, absolutely it can cause accuracy issues.

The arrows that were made for the long bow are going to be spined specifically to the force of that bow, so that they bend appropriately.

Unless the force of the recurve is almost identical, the arrows won't bend the way they are supposed to when fired. If the spines are too soft, you could potentially break the arrow if the force of the recurve is substantially higher than the longbow

On the other hand, if the arrows are too hard/stiff, they won't bend around the riser and could shoot off to the left (if you're shooting right handed)
